en: When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with great qualities. Blessed One, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite qualities. Blessed One, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with boundless qualities. The Blessed One said: "So it is."

7. "So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with great qualities; Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite qualities.
8. Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with boundless qualities. Why is that? Because he has attained an infinite and limitless knowledge that is not shared [with others]."
9. Abiding in that knowledge, the irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva brings forth the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
By means of these analytical knowledges, even when questioned by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, he cannot be exhausted by his replies. Subhūti said:

"10. Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, is capable of [explaining] the forms, marks, and signs of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva for eons equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā."
To explain:
by which aspects, by which marks, and by which signs an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is characterized.
Excellent, Blessed One! The most profound points should be explained,
wherein abiding, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness,
up to and including omniscience.
[Subhūti] fulfilled [this]. The Blessed One said:

"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is indeed excellent, Subhūti, that for the sake of the irreversible Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, you have questioned the Tathāgata regarding these most profound points which are designations."
"That is to say, of nirvāṇa.
He said,
"Venerable Lord, this is indeed a designation for nirvāṇa alone, and not for all dharmas."
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, even for all dharmas, this is a designation: 'profound.
For what reason? Because..."

Subhūti, form is profound; Subhūti, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are profound. Subhūti, even the eye is profound, up to and including the mind, Subhūti, which is also profound; even awakening, Subhūti, is profound.
And how, Subhūti, is form profound?
It is profound in the same way that the suchness of form is profound; it is profound in the same way that the suchness of feeling is [profound].

As is the suchness of perception and of volitional formations, so is the suchness of consciousness; as is its suchness, so is it profound. Up to: as is the suchness of awakening, so is it profound. He asked: "Blessed One, what is the suchness of form, up to what is the suchness of awakening?"
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, where there is suchness of form, there is no form, nor is suchness elsewhere than from form; and so on, Subhūti, where there is suchness of consciousness, there is no consciousness, nor is suchness elsewhere than from consciousness; and so on, where there is suchness of awakening, there is no awakening..."
There is no suchness other than awakening.
He said:
"It is marvelous, Blessed One, how this irreversible [bodhisattva] is characterized by such a subtle means."

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has been turned away from form and pointed toward nirvāṇa; he has been turned away from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness and pointed toward nirvāṇa; and he has been turned away from all grasping, whether mundane or supramundane, common or uncommon.
Having turned [him] away from the tainted and the untainted and having indicated Nirvana, the Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who shall contemplate, weigh, and reflect upon these most profound points associated with the perfection of wisdom..."
"In this way I must abide;

in the manner commanded in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, thus I must train; in the manner taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Subhūti, it is by accomplishing exactly as it is declared in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, by contemplating it thus, by examining it thus, by applying himself thus, by striving thus, and by exerting himself thus that this bodhisattva mahāsattva [proceeds]."
As it is taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
"By a single production of the thought [of awakening], one will grasp incalculable,
immeasurable, and infinite roots of virtue."
He will cast off immeasurable eons of saṃsāra;
how much more so for one who, practicing the perfection of wisdom without distraction, dwells with mental attentions associated with awakening?

"Subhūti, it is just as if there were a man of lustful temperament and discursive thought who had made an appointment with a certain woman—one who was beautiful, graceful, and lovely to behold—but that woman was under the protection of another and could not leave her home. What do you think, Subhūti? With what would the thoughts of that man be associated?"
He said:
"Blessed One, that man's thoughts would be connected only with women: 'She comes here; she has arrived; I shall sit with her; I shall dally with her. The Blessed One said: 'In that case...'"
"What do you think, Subhūti? With the passing of a night and the passing of a day, how many thoughts would arise in that man? He replied, "Many, Blessed One;
many, Sugata, would be the thoughts that would arise in that man with the passing of a night and the passing of a day."
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, as many thoughts as might arise for that person during the passing of a night and a day, for so many eons does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cast off and turn his back upon saṃsāra, if he should train here in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught."
He examines and reflects upon it,
and applies himself to yoga in such a way that he abandons those faults.

Subhūti, by those faults through which a bodhisattva mahāsattva would turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is thus devoted to yoga and dwells in this dwelling as taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā* [would turn back] in a single day.

Whatever root of merit he grasps, even if world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā were filled with it, that would not approach even a hundredth part of that root of merit, nor a thousandth part,
nor a hundred-thousandth part.
Furthermore, it does not even approach a number, a fraction, a calculation, a comparison, or a likeness.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom might give gifts to the Three Jewels for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā.

"In the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha—what do you think, Subhūti, would that bodhisattva mahāsattva generate much merit on that account? He replied, "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata; immeasurable, incalculable, boundless, and incomparable. The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, this very bodhisattva mahāsattva would generate a far greater amount of merit than that one who practices yoga here in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught.
Why is that? Because this is the method of the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, by which method they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

What do you think, Subhūti? If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom, were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, and were to establish offerings among those who have entered the stream, among once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas— what do you think, Subhūti?
"Would that bodhisattva mahāsattva, on that account, produce much merit? He replied, "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:

Subhūti, this very son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit on that basis who should apply themselves to yoga in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught.
Why is that? Because here, in the perfection of wisdom, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing, transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
He enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
What do you think, Subhūti? Suppose a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom, were to remain and live for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges.
"If one were to give gifts, guard morality, accomplish patience, exert vigor, enter the meditative concentrations, and cultivate wisdom—would that person, on that account, generate much merit?
He replied, "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata. The Blessed One said, "More than that..."

"Subhūti, a son of good family or a daughter of good family would generate much greater merit if, abiding here in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, they were to practice giving for even a single day, maintain ethical discipline,
accomplish patience, and exert vigor."
One should enter the twelve meditative absorptions and cultivate wisdom. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is the mother of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas; indeed, this perfection of wisdom is the progenitor of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas.
In this regard, Subhūti,
by abiding in this perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva mahāsattvas fulfill all dharmas,
until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"What do you think, Subhūti? If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom, were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā and bestow the gift of Dharma, would that son of good family or daughter of good family produce much merit on that account? He said, "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata. The Blessed One said:
Therefore, Subhūti,
that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit who,
abiding here in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, were to practice the gift of Dharma for even a single day.

One should give it. For what reason? Because, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is devoid of the perfection of wisdom is devoid of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). But, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who is not devoid of omniscience is not devoid of it. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should strive for] unsurpassed...
One who desires to fully awaken to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment must not be separated from the perfection of wisdom.

What do you think, Subhūti? If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were separated from the perfection of wisdom and, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, were to apply himself to the four foundations of mindfulness, up to emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and even apply himself to all meditative concentrations—[would he be able to attain it]?
"What do you think, Subhūti? Would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account? He said, "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata. The Blessed One said:

Subhūti, this very son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit who, for even a single day, should apply themselves to yoga in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught— [practicing] from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Why is that?
Subhūti, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is not separated from the perfection of wisdom should turn back from omniscience;
such a thing cannot occur.
Furthermore, Subhūti, it is indeed possible that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom, might turn back from omniscience;
this possibility exists.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must not be separated from the perfection of wisdom.

What do you think, Subhūti? If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom, were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, and were to dedicate toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment that gift of material things, that gift of Dharma, and those mental attentions associated with meditative seclusion— would that son of good family or daughter of good family, on that account, [produce much merit]?
[The Blessed One] said: "He would produce much merit.
[Śāriputra] said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:

Therefore, Subhūti, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit who, abiding here in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, for a single day were to dedicate toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment a gift of material things, a gift of the Dharma, and those mental non-attendings associated with solitary retreat. Why is that? Because this is the supreme dedication.
That is to say, it is the dedication by means of the perfection of wisdom; furthermore, any dedication that is without the perfection of wisdom is not a true dedication.

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment must become skilled in the dedication of roots of merit through the perfection of wisdom.
What do you think, Subhūti?
Suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom, were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā,
[making offerings] to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, together with their assemblies of śrāvakas.
If one were to dedicate all that root of merit toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
He replied: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata. The Blessed One said:

Therefore, Subhūti, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate a much greater amount of merit who, abiding here in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, were to dedicate even a single day’s root of goodness toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom precedes all dedications. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should] toward unsurpassed...
One who desires to fully awaken to unexcelled perfect enlightenment must be skilled in the dedication of the perfection of wisdom.
He said:
"But, Blessed One, since conditioned activity has been described by the Blessed One as conceptual construction, how then can that son of good family or daughter of good family..."
Or he would produce even more merit than that. And, Blessed One, it is possible through non-conditioning to give rise to right view,
to enter the state of certainty, to attain the fruit of stream-entry, and so on, up to awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Blessed One said:

"So it is, Subhūti, so it is. For indeed, without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), it is not possible to produce right view, to enter the state of certainty (*nyāma*), to attain the fruit of stream-entry, or even to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Moreover, Subhūti, even that gift of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom appears as empty, it appears as void, it appears as insubstantial, and it appears as pithless. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is well-trained in internal emptiness.
He is well-trained in external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness,

great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of all phenomena.

Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who is well-trained in the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—
having established himself in these emptinesses, however he examines those conditioned phenomena, [he does so correctly].
In whatever way the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not separated from the perfection of wisdom,
in that very way, as the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not separated from the perfection of wisdom,
so it is.
"He generates incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite merit.
Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, what is the distinction between the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), the immeasurable (*aprameya*), and the infinite (*aparimāṇa*)? The Blessed One replied:
"Subhūti, even that which is incalculable does not come within the range of calculation."
"Subhūti, whether in the conditioned realm or the unconditioned realm, it is 'immeasurable' (aprameya), Subhūti, because no measure can be found for it among past, future, or present phenomena.
It is 'limitless' (aparimāṇa), Subhūti, because it cannot be measured. He asked: "Blessed One, could there be a way in which even form (rūpa) is incalculable (asaṃkhyeya)?"
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness would be immeasurable, infinite, and incalculable; they would be immeasurable, infinite, and limitless. The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, there may be a way [in which this is so]."

"In what manner, Blessed One, would form also be incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite; and in what manner would feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also be incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite? He said: "By what manner, Blessed One, would form also..."
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness would also be incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite; they too would be incalculable and immeasurable. The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, form also is empty, incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite."
"Subhūti, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also empty, incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite," he said.

"But, Blessed One, is it only form that is empty, and only feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are empty? Are not all dharmas also empty? The Blessed One replied: "They are."

"What do you think, Subhūti? Have I not declared that all dharmas are empty? He replied, "Blessed One, all dharmas have been declared empty by the Tathāgata. And that which is emptiness, Blessed One, is also inexhaustible; it is immeasurable; it is infinite. For, Blessed One, no number is found in emptiness, nor is a measure or a limit found."
"Therefore, Blessed One, no distinction is perceived among these dharmas, whether by way of meaning or by way of phrasing.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is. No distinction is perceived among these dharmas, whether in their meaning or in their phrasing.
This, Subhūti, is inexpressible, yet it has been expressed by the Tathāgata as 'inexhaustible' or as 'immeasurable.'"
Whether it be "emptiness," or "signlessness," or "wishlessness," or "the unconditioned," or "non-arising," or "dispassion," or "cessation," or "nirvāṇa"—
this is the Tathāgata’s teaching, its accomplishment, and its exposition, from "the inexhaustible" up to "nirvāṇa.
He said:
It is marvelous, Blessed One, how this true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) has been taught by the Tathāgata as inexpressible.
As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken:
“Blessed One, all phenomena are indeed inexpressible.
The Blessed One said, “So it is, Subhūti; so it is. Subhūti, all phenomena are inexpressible. That which is the inexpressibility of phenomena, Subhūti, is [the nature of phenomena].”
"Emptiness is not something that can be expressed within emptiness, nor is emptiness capable of being expressed.
He asked: "But, Blessed One, is there any increase or decrease in an inexpressible reality?
The Blessed One replied:
"Indeed not so, Subhūti; indeed not so, Subhūti. There is neither increase nor decrease of that meaning which is ineffable. Subhūti said:
Furthermore, Blessed One, if there is neither increase nor decrease in that ineffable reality, then, Blessed One, there will be neither increase nor decrease in the perfection of generosity;

there will likewise be neither increase nor decrease in the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom. And for the four applications of mindfulness, up to the noble eightfold path, there will be neither increase nor decrease.

of the path, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
There will be neither increase nor decrease;
there will be an absence of the six perfections,
up to and including an absence of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
And because of the non-existence of these dharmas, there will also be the non-existence of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Because of the non-existence of the knowledge of all aspects, who indeed would fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?
"Or will he fully awaken?
The Blessed One said, "So it is, Subhūti, so it is. There is neither increase nor decrease in that which is ineffable. He...

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom, cultivates the perfection of wisdom, and applies himself to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom is skillful in means, it does not occur to him: "I am increasing in the perfection of wisdom," and so on, up to: "I am increasing in the perfection of generosity."
Moreover, it occurs to him: "This which is called the perfection of giving is merely a name.

While practicing the perfection of giving, he dedicates those mental attentions, those productions of thought, and those roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; and he dedicates them in such a manner.

Just as with unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, so too, while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom, he dedicates those mental attentions, those productions of the thought of awakening, and those roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; and he dedicates them in such a manner.
Regarding the Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment, [Subhūti] asked: "Blessed One, how is it that there is unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?
The Blessed One replied:
"Subhūti, that which is the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) is unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, of which all phenomena is this suchness the unexcelled [enlightenment]?"

9. Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, that which is the suchness of form, up to and including the suchness of nirvāṇa—that is unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. It neither increases nor decreases. Subhūti, it is for this reason that a bodhisattva mahāsattva..."

One who dwells constantly and frequently, never separated from the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the increase or the decrease of any dharma whatsoever. Subhūti, it is because the ineffable reality neither increases nor decreases. Subhūti, in this very way, there is no increase whatsoever of the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom.
There is no diminution;
likewise, up to the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), there is neither increase nor diminution.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
By way of being neither increasing nor decreasing.
